A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same RL-based unmasking-policy study. Their complete main texts and appendices, including equations, tables and figures, support reliable matching despite additions and reorganization in v3.

before.justification: v1 reports original policy-training experiments, mathematical and coding benchmark evaluations, transfer experiments and ablations in Section 4 and Appendix A.

after.justification: v3 retains original experimental results and adds latency measurements, training-seed comparisons and analyses of generated token trajectories.

M1.justification: The confidence-input transformer, Bernoulli actions, GRPO objective, multiplicative reward, DPLS alternative and expert steering are retained. The added algorithm and implementation explanations document the existing procedure rather than establish a changed method.

E1.justification: Both versions use GSM8k, MATH/MATH-500, KodCode-RL-10K, HumanEval and MBPP, retaining model transfer, semi-AR/full-diffusion generation and length transfer to 512 tokens. The new trajectory analyses reuse existing GSM8k conditions rather than introduce new task coverage.

E2.justification: Random unmasking, High Confidence and Fast-dLLM remain the evaluated baselines in corresponding benchmark comparisons. DPLS and alternative policy-input comparisons also persist. Newly cited methods in Section 5 are not added as evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: Section 4.1 changes from averaging two training seeds to selecting one by final training loss, while retaining three test-time seeds. v3 also introduces wall-clock evaluation and a 100-example GSM8k trajectory-analysis protocol with token-order and adjacency measurements. These substantially extend evaluation design without establishing that all retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: New Appendices C and D investigate compute allocation across blocks, simultaneous unmasking of adjacent tokens, unmasking-order correlations and individual generation trajectories. Figure 13 additionally examines variation across training seeds. These add substantial behavioral and sensitivity analyses beyond v1's retained reward, likelihood, input and temperature ablations.

E5.justification: Main evaluation summaries change from averaging across training seeds to reporting a selected seed, altering their representation of training variability. v3 adds individual-seed scatter in Figure 13 and correlations reported with plus/minus values in Appendix C. The PDFs do not establish an increase in training-run counts.

E6.justification: Matched benchmark curves contain revised policy and comparator values, including the Dream results in v1 Figure 7 versus v3 Figure 11. Policy changes accompany the revised seed-selection protocol and cannot be treated as identical-protocol gains. Substantial new findings include latency results and approximately 20% versus 65% adjacent-token co-unmasking for the learned policy versus Fast-dLLM in Appendix C.1.

T1.justification: v3 Appendix G corrects the uniform-diffusion kernel to use alpha_t in both mixture terms; v1 Appendix E used alpha in the uniform term. Section 3.1 also changes the return-sum lower bound from zero to one. The DPLS derivation and expert-steering mathematics otherwise remain unchanged, with no new theorem or proof.

C1.justification: The introduction adds an explicit contribution that learned policies exhibit qualitatively different unmasking behavior from confidence heuristics. The central method and semi-AR/full-diffusion performance claims remain. The shortened abstract omits v1's transferability findings and associated caveats, although transfer remains discussed in the paper.

C2.justification: v3 adds substantive explanations involving dispersed unmasking, extra computation on final numerical answers, inflated padding-token confidence and expert steering recovering left-to-right generation. It also identifies wasted computation after EOS. Conversely, v1's explicit Dream-performance limitation and related future directions disappear from the conclusion, alongside revisions to the coding-transfer interpretation.

D1.justification: v3 adds inference pseudocode and architecture wiring, explains exclusion of already-unmasked positions from likelihood computation and termination of incomplete training generations, identifies d1 correctness rewards, and specifies A100 timing hardware. Existing training and architecture hyperparameter values in Table 1 remain unchanged.

R1.justification: Section 5 adds closely related GRPO unmasking work by Hong et al. (2025b), distinguishing its fixed token count from this method's adaptive actions. It also adds references on KLASS, calibration, speculative decoding and efficient reasoning, while removing some background references. The overall research positioning remains; publication-metadata updates are not new cited works.

P1.justification: The abstract and several background, method and experimental passages are condensed or locally rewritten, terminology shifts toward full-diffusion, and the appendices are reorganized. The six-section main narrative and much existing exposition remain intact. The author name João Monteiro is also corrected.

P2.justification: v3 adds policy and architecture diagrams, compute-allocation and unmasking-order plots, latency and seed-scatter displays, and extensive token-trajectory visualizations. Existing figures are relocated and receive grid, caption and labeling changes; the dense-alpha plot is connected by alpha to expose nonmonotonicity. This substantially expands the visual presentation beyond numerical updates.

improvement.justification: Compared with v1's NFE-based efficiency evidence and limited behavioral explanation, v3 provides measured latency, detailed sampling diagnostics and clearer implementation documentation. These improve support and interpretability. The gains are tempered by replacing training-seed averages with a selected seed and removing the explicit Dream limitation discussion; the new seed-scatter plot partly restores visibility into variability. The net quality improvement is useful but limited.
